nameStory: This butterfly carries the name of French naturalist Pierre-André Latreille's colleague, who first described the species in scientific literature. The "tortoiseshell" part comes from the rich, mottled orange and dark brown wing pattern that resembles the beautiful shell of a tortoise. Some people also call it the "fire-rim tortoiseshell" because of the bright orange bands that seem to glow like embers along the wing edges.
description: Milbert's Tortoiseshell is a medium-sized butterfly with striking orange and dark brown wings that create a warm, mottled pattern reminiscent of tortoiseshell jewelry. The wings typically span about 2-2.5 inches across and feature distinctive bright orange bands along the outer edges. This is the only tortoiseshell butterfly you'll find in New England, making it relatively easy to identify once you know what to look for. When the wings are closed, the underside is much darker and more camouflaged, helping the butterfly blend in when resting.

idTips.label: Orange wing bands
idTips.description: Look for bright orange bands running along the outer edges of both forewings and hindwings, creating a distinctive border that almost glows in sunlight

idTips.label: Dark wing base
idTips.description: The inner portions of the wings are dark brown to blackish, creating a strong contrast with the orange bands

idTips.label: Scalloped wing edges
idTips.description: Wing margins have a gently scalloped or wavy edge rather than being perfectly smooth, giving them a delicate, decorative appearance

idTips.label: Size and flight
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a somewhat erratic, bouncing flight pattern typical of tortoiseshells, often seen basking on rocks or tree trunks with wings spread wide

idTips.label: Underside coloring
idTips.description: When wings are folded, the underside appears much darker and mottled, providing excellent camouflage against tree bark or rock surfaces

habitat: Milbert's Tortoiseshell prefers open woodlands, forest edges, meadows, and gardens throughout New England's mountains and foothills. You'll often spot them in areas where stinging nettles grow, as these plants serve as their primary host for egg-laying. They're particularly common in the northern parts of New England and at higher elevations where cooler temperatures suit their preferences.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hibernation in April and May, often seen basking in sunny spots on warm days. Look for worn-looking individuals with faded colors from their long winter sleep.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time with fresh, bright adults most active from June through August. This is the best time to see their vibrant orange bands at full intensity as they feed on flowers and tree sap.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for hibernation by feeding heavily on late-season flowers and fermenting fruit. Colors may appear slightly duller as they seek sheltered spots under bark or in woodpiles.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected locations like loose bark, wood piles, or building crevices. Occasionally spotted on unusually warm winter days but generally inactive.

funFact: Milbert's Tortoiseshell adults can live for up to 10 months by hibernating through the winter as fully grown butterflies, making them one of the longest-lived butterflies in New England - much longer than most species that only live a few weeks as adults.
confusionNotes: The only other tortoiseshell in North America is the California Tortoiseshell, which doesn't occur in New England. The orange and brown pattern might remind some people of a small monarch butterfly, but monarchs are much larger, have black veining, and lack the scalloped wing edges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting European origins, Milbert's Tortoiseshell is actually the only North American member of the tortoiseshell genus Aglais. Most other tortoiseshells live in Europe and Asia, making this species a unique representative of its group on our continent.
compareHints: As the only Aglais species in North America, Milbert's Tortoiseshell is quite distinct from its European cousin, the European Peacock Butterfly, which has large eyespots on its wings. Within the brush-footed butterfly family in New England, it's most similar to the Mourning Cloak, but Mourning Cloaks are larger, darker overall, and have a yellow border instead of orange. The Compton Tortoiseshell, while in a different genus, is much larger and has more muted, grayish coloring rather than the bright orange bands.
